summary: RotateWise is a free website that helps Iowa farmers and their county extension agents decide which crop rotations deserve a closer conversation. It starts from a simple idea: the same summer doesn’t hurt every field in the same way, because the timing of a crop’s critical growth matters as much as the crop itself. We trained a model on 26 years of NASA POWER weather and USDA yields for all 99 Iowa counties to learn which summer months expose a field most. RotateWise then compares three rotations by how much of each crop’s critical growth falls in those months, and by how long soil sits bare during storm season. Visitors set their own priorities (water, soil health, income, labour) and watch the ranking respond, with the evidence, information gaps and risks behind every option. It is a hindcast, not a forecast, and it supports local expertise rather than replacing it. We tested on held-back years and report plainly where the model helps, where it only modestly beats a simple baseline, and where it fails.
details:
RotateWise brings NASA Earth observation data to a decision Iowa farmers and their extension agents face every year: which crop rotation is worth exploring next. A visitor chooses a county, confirms the current rotation and sets four priorities: water, soil health, income and labour. The app then walks them through four steps (Your county, What hurts yields, Your options, Talk it over). It returns three strategies ranked with a transparent formula, each with its rationale, supporting evidence, possible benefits and the questions to bring to a local expert.

Behind the interface sits a rigorously validated model. We combined 26 years of NASA POWER daily weather with USDA yield records for all 99 Iowa counties and trained a monotone generalized additive model that learns which summer conditions pull yields away from trend. SHAP values turn that model into a month-by-month stress profile. For corn, July carries about 65% of the weather sensitivity. RotateWise then compares rotations by how much of each crop’s critical growth falls in those months, and by how long soil is left bare during storm season.

We held the work to research-grade standards. Our model-selection rule was written before the first result came in. We evaluated with leave-one-year-out cross-validation, 90% bootstrap intervals, a placebo test, a spatial hold-out and a fully blind test on 2025. Over the held-back years, corn error fell from 9.2 to 8.2 percentage points against a trend-only baseline. In 2025, the model’s statewide corn estimate was +3.1% against +3.3% actual. An Evidence section puts the model through stress tests on the 2012 drought and the 2020 derecho, using NASA MODIS vegetation data, the US Drought Monitor, NOAA storm reports and USDA crop-insurance records.

The benefit is a county-specific, evidence-based starting point for a conversation that is usually shaped by habit and averages. Because rankings shift with a farmer’s priorities, we show how often each strategy comes out on top across 2,000 random priority mixes, so the result never looks arbitrary. The tool is built to support farmer judgment and local expertise, and it is free, fast and open to anyone with a browser. The site scored 100 on Lighthouse accessibility and best practices.

We built it in Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, LightGBM, pyGAM, SHAP, GeoPandas) and React with TypeScript, deployed on Vercel. Every number is precomputed, so the finished site is static, with no server, live model or external API. Automated tests confirm that the browser’s scoring matches our Python scoring exactly. The data came from NASA POWER, NASA MODIS via ORNL DAAC, USDA NASS, USDA RMA, USDA-NRCS, the US Drought Monitor, NOAA and the US Census Bureau. The team of three completed the build over a single weekend, November 14-15, 2026.

What we added ourselves is the link between machine learning and the agronomic calendar. The model’s explanations become a stress profile, and rotations are compared by exposure in the months that matter, not by an invented yield. We also built the priority-sensitivity view, and we scored only criteria with sourced evidence, so every score can be traced to a citation.

We designed around trust and transparency. We logged and link-audited every source, made the pipeline fully reproducible, kept farmer judgment at the center, and documented our use of AI tools in the repository.
